passages.title: Malonyl-CoA and the direction of fatty acid flux in hepatocytes
paragraphs: Fatty acids are assembled in the cytosol and dismantled in the mitochondrial matrix, and a hepatocyte must not run both pathways at once. Synthesis begins when acetyl-CoA carboxylase converts acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA, which is the committed step; fatty acid synthase then adds malonyl units to a growing chain two carbons at a time, using NADPH as the reductant, and releases palmitate after seven rounds of condensation and reduction. Oxidation begins instead with the transfer of a long-chain acyl group from coenzyme A to carnitine by carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 (CPT-1) in the outer mitochondrial membrane, and continues through cycles that reduce FAD and NAD+ and release acetyl-CoA. Malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-1, so the molecule that commits carbon to synthesis also closes the door to oxidation. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase is activated by citrate and is inhibited when AMP-activated protein kinase phosphorylates it.

Hepatocyte monolayers were incubated for 60 minutes in a medium containing labelled acetate and, in parallel dishes, labelled palmitate. Synthesis was scored as label recovered in cellular palmitate, and oxidation as label recovered in acid-soluble products and in CO₂. Five conditions were compared: medium alone; medium with insulin; medium with compound K, an activator of AMP-activated protein kinase; medium with an inhibitor of acetyl-CoA carboxylase; and medium with that inhibitor together with an inhibitor of CPT-1. Cytosolic malonyl-CoA was measured in a separate extract from the same dishes (Table 1).

Cell ATP content, total protein and the activity of the pentose phosphate pathway that supplies NADPH differed by less than 8% across the five conditions, and no condition reduced the number of attached cells. Labelled acetate entered the cells at the same rate in every condition, so the differences in Table 1 reflect the fate of carbon inside the cell rather than its entry.

passages.title: Ion currents in the ventricular action potential
paragraphs: A ventricular myocyte at rest sits near the potassium equilibrium potential because an inward rectifier potassium channel holds the membrane there. A depolarisation that reaches threshold opens fast sodium channels, and their current drives the upstroke of phase 0; the steepness of that upstroke is a direct reading of how much fast sodium current is available. The channels then inactivate, and a transient outward potassium current produces the small notch of phase 1. Through the long plateau of phase 2, inward current through L-type calcium channels is nearly balanced by outward potassium current, and the calcium that enters triggers release of further calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Phase 3 repolarisation is carried by delayed rectifier potassium channels, and phase 4 returns the cell to rest. Fast sodium channels recover from inactivation only once the membrane has repolarised, and the fraction available at rest falls steeply as the resting potential becomes less negative.

Myocytes were isolated from adult ventricle and action potentials were recorded with a microelectrode at 37 °C while the cells were driven at one beat per second. Each of four compounds was then added to a separate dish at a concentration that blocks a single channel type. For every recording the investigators measured the maximum rate of rise of phase 0, the time from the upstroke to 90% repolarisation, and the resting potential reached between beats (Table 1).

In the control recordings the membrane rose from its resting potential to an overshoot near +30 mV, fell to a plateau near +5 mV, and repolarised over the following 300 ms. The amplitude of the plateau and the overshoot at the peak were unchanged by drugs W and Y, and no compound altered the resting potential except drug Z, which was applied at a concentration that blocks the inward rectifier without acting on any other channel.

passages.title: Antibiotic inhibition of translation in cell-free extracts
paragraphs: A bacterial ribosome is a 70S particle built from a 30S subunit, whose 16S ribosomal RNA forms the decoding centre that checks each codon-anticodon pair, and a 50S subunit, whose 23S ribosomal RNA forms the peptidyl transferase centre and the tunnel through which the new chain leaves. The eukaryotic cytosolic ribosome is an 80S particle built from a 40S and a 60S subunit. The catalytic cores of the two ribosomes are built from homologous RNA, but the surfaces around them differ, and most clinically useful inhibitors of translation exploit those differences rather than the catalytic site itself.

Five compounds were tested in a cell-free system. A single synthetic messenger RNA encoding a protein of 100 amino acid residues, including the initiator methionine, was translated either in an extract of bacterial cells or in an extract of rabbit reticulocytes, both supplied with transfer RNA, amino acids and an energy source. Incorporation of a labelled amino acid into acid-precipitable protein was measured after 20 minutes and is expressed as a percentage of the incorporation in the same extract with no compound added. The subunit each compound binds was determined separately by equilibrium binding to purified subunits (Table 1).

Two further results were obtained with the bacterial extract. Compound 1 raised the incorporation of an amino acid whose codon was absent from the messenger RNA by about eightfold, while the other four compounds left it unchanged. After treatment with compound 3, the eukaryotic extract retained its ribosomes on the messenger RNA as polysomes rather than releasing them, whereas compound 2 left the bacterial messenger RNA almost free of ribosomes.

passages.title: Methylation and histone acetylation at a silenced reporter
paragraphs: Cytosines that sit immediately 5' of a guanosine can carry a methyl group, added by a DNA methyltransferase. Dense methylation of such sites in a promoter is associated with silence, and it acts indirectly: proteins that bind methylated cytosine recruit histone deacetylases, which strip acetyl groups from the lysine side chains of histone tails. A deacetylated tail carries more positive charge, binds DNA more tightly, and leaves the promoter inaccessible to transcription factors. Two methyltransferase activities exist: one copies an existing pattern onto the new strand after replication, acting only where the parent strand is already methylated, and one places methyl groups on sites that carry no mark at all.

A reporter gene driven by a promoter rich in these sites was integrated at a single chromosomal position in a cultured line, where it was almost silent. Cells were treated for 72 hours with nothing, with a cytosine analogue that is incorporated into DNA but cannot be methylated, with an inhibitor of histone deacetylases, or with both drugs together. Reporter messenger RNA was then measured (Figure 1). In the same cells the share of the promoter's cytosine-guanosine sites carrying a methyl group was 80% untreated, 15% after the cytosine analogue, 78% after the deacetylase inhibitor and 14% after both drugs; acetylated histone at the promoter, measured by immunoprecipitation and expressed relative to untreated cells, was 1.0, 3.5, 6.0 and 7.0 in the same four conditions.

Reporter copy number and the sequence of the promoter were identical in all four conditions, and a second reporter driven by a promoter with few such sites gave the same expression whichever treatment was used. When the cytosine analogue was washed out and the cells were grown for 20 further divisions, methylation of the first promoter returned to 79% and the reporter fell silent again.

passages.title: Signals that commit a multipotent progenitor
paragraphs: A multipotent mesenchymal progenitor can give rise to bone, cartilage or fat, and which path it takes is decided by signals from outside the cell that converge on a small number of master transcription factors. The factor RUNX2 is required for the osteogenic programme and switches on the genes whose products mineralise the surrounding matrix; the nuclear receptor PPAR-gamma is required for the adipogenic programme and switches on the genes of lipid storage. A progenitor that has committed to either path divides more slowly than one that has not, and a progenitor can also divide without committing at all, which is how the population maintains itself.

Cells of a clonal progenitor line were plated at a density low enough that each colony arose from one cell, and were grown for 10 days in a defined medium with no added signals, with a bone morphogenetic protein, with insulin together with an agonist of PPAR-gamma, with both sets of signals, or with the bone morphogenetic protein together with a small-molecule inhibitor of RUNX2. Every colony was then scored as mineralised, as containing lipid droplets, or as undifferentiated, and the population doubling time was measured in parallel flasks (Table 1).

No colony in any condition was scored both mineralised and lipid-laden, and no condition reduced the number of colonies formed, so the proportions in Table 1 are drawn from populations of the same size. Expression of RUNX2 messenger RNA rose about fifteenfold in the cultures given the bone morphogenetic protein, whether or not the RUNX2 inhibitor was present, because the inhibitor blocks the activity of the protein rather than its production.

passages.title: Oxidation of a test drug by liver microsomes
paragraphs: Most drugs that reach the liver are first oxidised by a cytochrome P450 enzyme of the endoplasmic reticulum, a haem protein that splits molecular oxygen and inserts one atom into the substrate while reducing the other to water. The electrons come from NADPH by way of a flavoprotein reductase, so an oxidation of this kind cannot proceed without the reduced cofactor. The hydroxylated product is usually more water soluble than the parent drug, and a second set of enzymes then conjugates it to glucuronic acid or sulfate for excretion. The amount of a P450 enzyme in the liver is not fixed: several drugs raise it by increasing transcription of its gene, an effect that takes days to develop and days to reverse.

Microsomes were prepared from the livers of rats in four groups: untreated animals; animals given an inducing drug daily for five days; untreated animals whose microsomes were assayed with a second drug present in the cuvette; and untreated animals whose assay mixture contained no NADPH. Formation of the hydroxylated metabolite of a test drug was followed at eight substrate concentrations between 1 and 200 micromolar, and the rates were fitted to the Michaelis-Menten equation to give the values in Table 1. The amount of the enzyme in each preparation was measured independently with an antibody against it.

No metabolite at all was formed in the preparation lacking NADPH, at any substrate concentration, so no Michaelis constant could be fitted for it. The second drug was present at a fixed concentration throughout, and the fit was good at every substrate concentration tested.

passages.title: Calcium and the regulation of tension in a smooth muscle strip
paragraphs: Smooth muscle has no troponin. A rise in cytosolic Ca²⁺ is read instead by calmodulin, and the calcium-calmodulin complex activates myosin light chain kinase, which phosphorylates the regulatory light chain of myosin and so permits cross-bridge cycling. A myosin light chain phosphatase works continuously in the opposite direction, and the level of phosphorylation at any moment is set by the balance of the two. That balance can be shifted without any change in calcium: an agonist acting through a G protein can activate a Rho-associated kinase that inhibits the phosphatase, so that a given calcium concentration produces more phosphorylation and more tension. Calcium itself reaches the cytosol both through voltage-gated channels in the plasma membrane and from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which releases it when IP₃ is generated at the membrane.

Strips of vascular smooth muscle were mounted at fixed length so that tension could be recorded without shortening, and cytosolic Ca²⁺ was followed with a fluorescent indicator in the same strips. Each strip was exposed to one stimulus: no stimulus; an agonist at 10 nM in normal medium; the same agonist in a medium from which Ca²⁺ had been omitted; the agonist with an inhibitor of myosin light chain kinase; the agonist with an inhibitor of Rho-associated kinase; or 60 mM potassium chloride, which depolarises the membrane and opens voltage-gated channels without acting on any receptor. Peak values are given in Table 1, with tension expressed as a percentage of the maximum the strip could develop.

The indicator was calibrated in each strip before the stimulus was applied, and the calibration did not differ between strips. Neither inhibitor altered the peak calcium reached, and no strip shortened by more than 2% of its resting length during a contraction.

passages.title: Mutants defective in biofilm formation
paragraphs: Free-swimming bacteria that meet a surface may attach to it reversibly using a flagellum or pili, then attach irreversibly and secrete an exopolysaccharide matrix that holds the growing community together. The genes of that matrix are switched on only when the population is dense, which the cells judge by the concentration of a small diffusible autoinducer that each of them makes and releases: the molecule accumulates as the cells accumulate, and above a threshold it activates its regulator and the matrix genes with it. A mature biofilm tolerates antibiotics far better than the same cells in suspension, partly because the matrix slows the drug's approach and partly because cells deep inside the film divide slowly, and most antibiotics kill only cells that are growing.

A wild-type strain and three mutants were grown without shaking in plastic wells for 24 hours. The mutants lacked, respectively, the flagellum, the enzyme that makes the matrix exopolysaccharide, and the enzyme that synthesises the autoinducer; the last strain was also tested with the autoinducer supplied in the medium from the start. Biofilm biomass was measured as the dye retained by the well after the planktonic cells had been rinsed away (Figure 1). Growth in suspension, measured as optical density after eight hours of shaken culture, was 0.80, 0.78, 0.82 and 0.79 for the wild type and the three mutants in the order given, and 0.80 for the autoinducer-supplied culture.

Each strain was then exposed for four hours to an antibiotic, either as an intact biofilm or as planktonic cells from a shaken culture of the same strain. For the wild type, 40% of the biofilm cells survived against 0.5% of its planktonic cells. For the matrix-deficient mutant, 2% of the cells in the well survived against 0.6% of its planktonic cells.

passages.title: Patterns in the thyroid axis of five people
paragraphs: Thyrotropin-releasing hormone from the hypothalamus drives the pituitary thyrotrophs to secrete thyroid-stimulating hormone, and that hormone drives the thyroid follicular cell to trap iodide, build thyroglobulin, and release mostly thyroxine with a little triiodothyronine. Only a small share of circulating triiodothyronine comes from the gland; most is made where it acts, by removal of one iodine atom from thyroxine. Free hormone, not the much larger protein-bound fraction, inhibits secretion at both the pituitary and the hypothalamus, so a healthy axis holds free thyroxine in a narrow band and the concentration of thyroid-stimulating hormone is the most sensitive index of whether it is being held.

Five people were studied with the same assays on the same day. One was healthy. In one the thyroid had been destroyed by autoimmune disease; in one a pituitary tumour was secreting thyroid-stimulating hormone without regard to feedback; one was taking a large daily dose of thyroxine by mouth; and in one the pituitary had been damaged and could secrete almost no thyroid-stimulating hormone. Which person was which was not disclosed to the laboratory. Each then received an injection of thyrotropin-releasing hormone, and the rise in thyroid-stimulating hormone 30 minutes later was recorded as a fold change over that person's own baseline (Table 1).

The reference range of the laboratory was 0.4 to 4.0 mIU/L for thyroid-stimulating hormone, 12 to 22 pmol/L for free thyroxine and 3.0 to 6.5 pmol/L for free triiodothyronine. Total thyroxine, which includes the much larger bound fraction, moved in the same direction as free thyroxine in every subject, and the concentration of the binding proteins was normal in all five.

passages.title: Pattern-recognition receptors in cultured macrophages
paragraphs: The innate response to a microbe begins with receptors that recognise molecules shared by whole classes of organism rather than by one strain: the lipopolysaccharide of a Gram-negative outer membrane, a bacterial lipopeptide, double-stranded RNA of the kind made during viral replication. These receptors are encoded in the germline and are the same in every cell of a given type, which is why the response is immediate and why it is identical on a second encounter. Some of them sit in the plasma membrane and meet their ligand outside the cell; others sit in the membrane of an endosome and meet their ligand only after it has been taken up, and their signalling depends on the acidification of that compartment. Whichever receptor is engaged, the signal passes through an adaptor protein to a transcription factor held inactive in the cytosol, which then enters the nucleus and switches on cytokine genes.

Macrophage lines were derived from a wild-type mouse and from three mutant lines lacking, respectively, receptor P, receptor Q and adaptor R. Each line was stimulated for six hours with bacterial lipopolysaccharide, with a synthetic double-stranded RNA, or with both together, and the cytokine secreted into the medium was measured (Table 1). Unstimulated cultures of every line secreted less than 50 pg/mL.

In a further experiment, wild-type cells were given a compound that prevents endosomes from acidifying. Their response to double-stranded RNA fell to 150 pg/mL, while their response to lipopolysaccharide was 4000 pg/mL, close to the untreated value. The compound did not alter the number of viable cells over six hours, and all four lines grew at the same rate in the absence of any stimulus.
